newsitem.title: USA: Post-EMU FX reserves unlikely to hit dlr-euro rate.
newsitem.headline: Post-EMU FX reserves unlikely to hit dlr-euro rate.

text.p: Any surplus in central bank reserves resulting from the introduction of a single European currency is unlikely to have a major impact on exchange rates, European officials and economists said on Tuesday.

"Assuming there are a lot of excess reserves (at the launch of Economic and Monetary Union) there are two things that cannot happen," Jean Jacques Rey, Executive Director of the Bank of Belgium, told a conference.

"One is a softer monetary policy than otherwise because of reserve ease," he said. "The second thing that cannot happen is that the system would start to sell excess reserves outright in the market," he said.
With the launch of a single currency in 1999, EMU members will no longer have to stabilise their exchange rates among themselves and their demand for reserves is likely to decline.
Some central bank reserves will also be pooled by the future European Central Bank.
As a result, European banks could face a surplus of dollars or marks, which if dumped too quickly on foreign exchange markets, would have a major impact on the dollar-euro exchange rate.

But experts at a discussion sponsored by The Reinventing Bretton Woods Committee said the future European Central Bank would steer clear of disposing any surplus reserves in a way that would disrupt market.
"The focus on reserve assets strikes me as secondary at best, maybe tertiary," said John Lipsky, chief economist at U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers.

"It's not likely one would start with the presumption that central banks, which are after all not profit maximizing institutions, would seek to follow essentially narrow commercial needs if that implied destabilizing the markets," he added.
In the event reserve disposal was necessary, Rey said yet-to-be defined guidelines would prevent national central banks from acting unilaterally in the run-up to EMU.
"It's easy to guess (the guidelines) will make sure that the behavior of national central bank authorities does not disturb markets," he said.

Economists say that allocation of assets towards the new euro zone and the expected deep liquidity of the new bond market in euros may play a more significant role in influencing the dollar-euro exchange rate.
But they have not yet reached any real conclusions on what the effect will be.
